input: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures. At 300 K, the value of $k$ was found to be 0.036 s-1, while at 340 K a value of $k$ of 0.53 s-1 was obtained, this latter figure being a derived value that was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 57 kJ mol-1. Each of the temperatures was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%, which gives an indication of the reproducibility of the measurements. Above 340 K, however, it was found that the solvent evaporated during sampling, and for this reason no rate constant is reported above that temperature. The two values that are reported illustrate the strong sensitivity of the rate constant to temperature over the interval that was studied, since the rate constant at the higher temperature is considerably larger than that at the lower temperature. It is worth noting that the value at the higher temperature rests on the Arrhenius relation and on the stated activation energy, rather than being a direct measurement of the same standing as the lower value. The upper end of the interval is therefore set by the failure of the sampling procedure rather than by the reaction itself, because evaporation during sampling removes solvent from the sample as it is withdrawn, meaning that a sample taken at a higher temperature would no longer have the composition of the reacting mixture, and any rate constant calculated from it would describe the sample rather than the reaction.
